> At the arrival of the rain clouds, ten times the square root of a flock of swans flew to Lake Manasa <term>Manasa</term> <gloss>the sacred Lake Manasarovar in the Himalayas</gloss>. One-eighth of the flock flew away from the water’s edge to a forest of land-lotuses. O young girl, three pairs of swans were seen playing in the water, which was beautiful with young lotus stalks. Tell me the total number of the entire flock.

**Connection of words:** O young girl! At the arrival of the clouds, ten times the square root <note>original: "mula-dashakam," ten times the root</note> of the flock of swans went to Lake Manasa. One-eighth part <term>ashtamshakah</term> <gloss>one-eighth</gloss> flew from the water's edge and went to a forest of land-lotuses. Three pairs of swans were seen playing in water beautiful with young lotus stalks. Therefore, tell the total number of the flock.

**Meaning:** O my dear one, sixteen years of age! <note>The word "Bala" refers to a young girl, often interpreted in this context as sixteen years old.</note> There was a flock of swans. From that group, when the rainy season arrived, ten times the square root of the total went to Lake Manasarovar. One-eighth part of the group flew from the edge of the water to a forest of land-lotuses. Three pairs of swans <note>amounting to six birds</note> were seen playing with great affection in water decorated with soft lotus roots. Say, how many swans were in that group?

**Mathematical Statement:** The root-multiplier <term>mula-gunam</term> is 10. The eighth part is <gloss>1/8</gloss>. The visible quantity <term>drishyam</term> <gloss>the known number of swans not associated with the root or fraction</gloss> is <gloss>6</gloss>. As it was stated that the quantity is "increased or decreased by fractions," we divide the visible quantity and the root-multiplier by the remainder of the fraction <note>calculated as 1 minus 1/8, which is 7/8</note>. This results in an adjusted visible quantity of <gloss>48/7</gloss> and an adjusted root-multiplier of <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Half of the multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. The square of this is <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. Adding the visible quantity <note>48/7, which is 336/49</note> to this gives <gloss>1936/49</gloss>. The square root of this is <gloss>44/7</gloss>. When this is joined with half the multiplier <gloss>40/7</gloss> and then squared, the resulting flock of swans <term>hansa-rashih</term> is 144.

**Detailed Working:** According to the rule mentioned in the previous verse, we subtract the eighth part <gloss>1/8</gloss> from one. Then <gloss>1/1 - 1/8</gloss> = <gloss>7/8</gloss>. We divide the visible quantity of 6 by this. <gloss>6/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>6/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>48/7</gloss>. Thus, 48/7 becomes the new visible quantity. Similarly, we divide the root-multiplier of 10 by 7/8. <gloss>10/1 divided by 7/8</gloss> = <gloss>10/1 × 8/7</gloss> = <gloss>80/7</gloss>. Now, taking 48/7 as the visible quantity and 80/7 as the root-multiplier, we perform the operation according to the method in the previous verse. That is, half of the root-multiplier is <gloss>40/7</gloss>. We square this, resulting in <gloss>1600/49</gloss>. We add this to the visible quantity 48/7 in the following way:

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse on the nature of the Supreme Being and the process of cosmic creation as described in the commentary on the Surya Siddhanta.</meta>

290

Surya Siddhanta

Vasudeva is the Supreme Brahman. His very form is the Supreme Person <note>original: Parama Purusha</note>; he is unmanifest, without qualities, peaceful, and beyond the twenty-five elements <note>referring to the twenty-five principles of the Samkhya school of philosophy</note> as well as immutable, which means he is without change. 12

->The God within nature, all-pervading outside and inside; Sankarshana, having created the waters first, cast his seed into them. 13<-

The text explains this because it is impossible for the pure Brahman to be the direct cause of the world. He is "within nature," meaning he is associated with <term>Maya</term> <gloss>the creative power of illusion</gloss>, and all-pervading because he is the material cause of the world. All these attributes are to be understood as belonging to Sankarshana, who is an expansion of Vasudeva, through the realization of their essential identity. Sankarshana, as an expansion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. Into those waters, he cast his "seed," which refers to a specific power or potency. 13

Lord Sankarshana, who is experienceable everywhere, entered within this very nature and first created the waters. Thereafter, he established his own brilliance in the form of a seed within that water. 13

->That became a golden egg, surrounded on all sides by darkness; there Aniruddha, the eternal, first became manifest. 14<-

The author then explains what happened next. That water, combined with that potency, became a <term>haimam</term> <gloss>golden</gloss> egg, spherical in shape, and was enveloped everywhere, inside and out, by darkness. The meaning is that the golden egg was produced in the sky accompanied by darkness. In that golden egg, first Aniruddha—the eternal, the expansion of Sankarshana and Vasudeva—became manifest. He was not "born" or "produced" in the literal sense, because the theory of <term>Satkaryavada</term> <gloss>the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in its cause</gloss> is accepted here. Just as oil is always present in sesame seeds and is merely manifested from them, he was manifested rather than created. 14

That seed-like brilliance took the form of a golden egg. It was surrounded on all sides by darkness. Within that egg, the eternal Lord Aniruddha first appeared. 14

->He is recited in the Vedas as the Lord Hiranyagarbha; because he is the first being, he is called Aditya, and by his procession he is called Surya. 15<-

Now the text provides his other names for the easy understanding of the people. This Lord Aniruddha, an expansion of Sankarshana and endowed with the <term>shāḍguṇya-aiśvarya</term> <gloss>six-fold lordly attributes of divinity</gloss>, is described in the <term>Chandas</term> <gloss>Vedas</gloss> as <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> <gloss>Golden Womb</gloss> because he resides in the womb or interior of the golden egg. This is his famous alternative name in the Vedas. He is certainly called <term>Aditya</term> <gloss>Son of Aditi or the First-born</gloss> because he was the first to be manifested. By his "procession," meaning his manifestation out of this world, he is called Surya.

"Hiranyagarbha was present in the beginning; when born, he was the sole lord of all created beings." <note>original Sanskrit quote from the Rig Veda 10.121.1: Hiranyagarbhah samavartatagre bhutasya jatah patireka asit</note> 15

This very person is Lord Hiranyagarbha who is mentioned in the Vedas. First of all...

This is indicated in the ritual section "The deities are spoken of" <note>referring to the Ashvalayana Shrauta Sutra 1.6</note>: "Agni and Soma, he who today... ## Hymn Text

**अग्नी॑षोमा॒ यो अ॒द्य वा॑मि॒दं वचः॑ स॒पर्य॑ति ।**
**तस्मै॑ धत्तं सु॒वीर्यं॒ गवां॒ पोषं॑ स्व॒श्व्य॑म् ॥ २ ॥**

->पदपाठः<-
**अग्नी॑षोमा । यः । अ॒द्य । वाम् । इ॒दम् । वचः॑ । स॒पर्य॑ति ।**
**तस्मै॑ । ध॒त्त॒म् । सु॒ऽवीर्य॑म् । गवा॑म् । पोष॑म् । सु॒ऽअश्व्य॑म् ॥ २ ॥**

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma**, whatever **sacrificer today** <note>during this ritual</note> **honors**—meaning treats as an object of worship—**this speech** <note>a sentence in the form of praise</note> **for you** <note>for both of you</note>, **bestow**—meaning grant—to **that** sacrificer the **increase** <note>the prosperity</note> of **cattle** <note>of livestock</note>. What kind of increase? **Great strength**, which is accompanied by excellent power and capability, and **good horses**, meaning it is joined with excellent horses. Regarding the word *gavām* <gloss>of cows</gloss>, the high accent usually expected on the case ending for monosyllabic stems is prohibited by the rule "not for the words *go* <note>cow</note> and *śvan* <note>dog</note> when followed by a vowel-ending case."

## Hymn Text

**अग्नी॑षोमा॒ य आहु॑तिं॒ यो वां॑ दा॒शाद्ध॑वि॒ष्कृति॑म् ।**
**स प्र॒जया॑ सु॒वीर्य॑म् वि॒श्वमायु॒व्य॑श्नवत् ॥ ३ ॥**

->पदपाठः<-
**अग्नी॑षोमा । यः । आ॒हुति॑म् । यः । वाम् । दाशा॑त् । ह॒विः॒ऽकृति॑म् ।**
**सः । प्र॒ऽजया॑ । सु॒ऽवीर्य॑म् । वि॒श्वम् । आयुः॑ । वि । अ॒श्न॒व॒त् ॥ ३ ॥**

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

O **Agni and Soma, whatever sacrificer should offer** <note>should give</note> **an oblation** <note>an offering of clarified butter</note> **to you** <note>to both of you</note>, or whatever sacrificer should give a **prepared offering** <note>an oblation made with sacrificial food such as rice-mash or cakes</note>, **that** sacrificer, possessing **great strength** <note>characterized by excellent power</note> along with **offspring** <note>sons, grandsons, and so on</note>, **may enjoy** <note>may attain</note> **all** <note>the entire</note> **life** <note>lifespan</note>. Regarding the word *āhutim* <gloss>oblation</gloss>, the suffix *ktin* is added to the root *hu* <note>to sacrifice</note>, and the word retains its original accent <term>prakṛti-svara</term>. The word *dāśāt* <gloss>may he give</gloss> is from the root *dāś* <note>to give</note>, using the Vedic subjunctive <term>leṭ</term> with the *āṭ* augment; it does not lose its accent because of its connection with the relative pronoun *yat* <note>who or whatever</note>. *Haviṣkṛtim* <gloss>prepared offering</gloss> refers to an offering where the preparation <term>kṛti</term> is of the sacrificial food <term>havis</term>; in this possessive compound <term>bahuvrīhi</term>, the first member retains its original accent.

# But by meditating on the Supreme, that which is hidden becomes manifest; for from Him come bondage and its opposite. [3.2.5]

Now, it might be argued that the <term>jiva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss> is a part of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of a fire. Since this is the case, just as the fire and the spark both possess the power to burn and to give light, the soul and the Lord should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Therefore, by the power of the soul's own knowledge and sovereignty, it should be able to create chariots and other objects in dreams through its mere will.

To this, we reply: even though the individual soul and the Lord stand in the relation of a part to the whole, it is a matter of direct perception that the soul possesses qualities opposite to those of the Lord.

Does this mean the soul does not possess the same qualities as the Lord at all? No, that is not the case. Although these qualities exist, they are hidden <note>original: "tirohitam"</note> because of the intervention of <term>avidya</term> <gloss>ignorance</gloss> and other factors. 

This hidden nature becomes manifest only in some individuals through the grace of God, as a result of meditating on the Supreme Lord and making an effort to dispel the darkness of ignorance. It is like the power of sight, which may be obstructed by a cataract but is restored through the power of medicine. This manifestation does not happen naturally for all living beings. Why? Because from Him, the Lord, come both the bondage and the liberation of the soul. Bondage results from the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of God, and liberation results from the realization of that nature.

As the scripture says: "By knowing the Divine, all bonds fall away; when the causes of suffering are destroyed, birth and death cease. By meditating on Him, a third state is reached when the body is cast off—universal sovereignty; he becomes the Absolute and his desires are fulfilled." <note>original: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>

# Or that obscuration also comes from the connection with the body. [3.2.6]

Why is it that the individual soul, being a part of the Supreme Self, has its knowledge and sovereignty hidden? It would be more logical for these qualities not to be hidden, just as the fire's power to burn and shine is not hidden in a spark.

We reply: while that may be true, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty happens because of its connection with the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the objects of perception. 

There is an analogy for this: just as the power of fire to burn and shine is hidden when it is latent within a piece of wood <note>original: "arani"</note>, or when it is covered by ash, the soul's qualities are hidden due to the connection with the body and other limiting conditions produced by names and forms which are set up by ignorance. This leads to the error of not discriminating between the Self and the body. 

The word "or" <note>original: "va"</note> in the sutra is used to refute the doubt that the soul is something other than the Lord. One might ask: "Why not simply say the soul is different from the Lord since its knowledge is hidden? Why imagine a connection with the body?" We say no: the soul's difference from the Lord cannot be proven. In the passage beginning "That Divinity thought," the scripture refers to the soul as the Self: "Entering with this living soul as the Self." <note>original: Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2</note> Furthermore, the scripture teaches the soul its identity with the Lord: "That is the Truth, that is the Self, Thou art That, O Shvetaketu." <note>original: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7</note> 

Therefore, being non-different from the Lord, the soul's knowledge and sovereignty are merely hidden by its connection with the body. Because of this, it is not possible for the soul to create chariots and other things in dreams by its own will. If a person could create through will in dreams, no one would ever see an unpleasant dream, for no one ever wills something unpleasant for themselves.

As for the argument that the scripture describes the dream state as being equal to the waking state to show its reality, that comparison is not intended to prove the reality of dreams. Such an interpretation would contradict the soul's self-luminous nature and the scriptural passages that state there are no actual chariots in dreams. The comparison is meant to show that dreams appear like the waking state because they are caused by the mental impressions <note>original: "vasanas"</note> produced during waking life. Therefore, it is established that the dream state is mere illusion <note>original: "maya-matratvam"</note>.

# Its absence takes place in the channels and in the Self, as is known from the scriptures. [3.2.7]

## The Section on the Absence of Dreams [Deep Sleep]

The state of dreaming has been examined. Now the state of deep sleep <note>original: "sushupti"</note> is examined. There are several scriptural passages concerning deep sleep. In one place it is said: "When he is thus asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream, then he has entered into these channels <note>original: "nadis"</note>." <note>original: Chandogya Upanishad 8.6.3</note> In another place, referring to the channels, it says: "Having crawled back through them, he rests in the pericardium <note>original: "puritat"</note>." <note>original: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.1.19</note>

Elsewhere, referring again to the channels, it says: "In them he rests when he is asleep and sees no dream; then he becomes one with the vital breath <note>original: "prana"</note> alone." In another passage: "He sleeps in the space within the heart." <note>original: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.1.17</note> In yet another: "Then, my dear, he is united with Being, he has gone to his own Self." <note>original: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.1</note> And also: "Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing without and nothing within." <note>original: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.3.21</note>

The doubt arises here: are these various locations like the channels and the rest to be considered independent and separate places for deep sleep, or are they to be considered together as a single location? 

What is the first view? That they are separate. Why? Because they serve the same purpose. Things that serve the same purpose are usually not dependent on one another...

<summary>Shankara explains that the individual soul's divine powers are hidden by its connection to the physical body and ignorance, meaning it cannot consciously create in dreams. The text then begins an inquiry into the nature and location of deep sleep according to various scriptures.</summary>

<keywords>jiva, ishvara, avidya, deep sleep, sushupti, dream state, maya, nadis, puritat, Shankara, Brahma Sutras</keywords>

# The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali
<meta>Sutras 48-49</meta>

## From that, there is speed of mind, the state beyond the body, and mastery over the Primary Cause. 48

Speed of mind <term>manojavitvam</term> is the body's attainment of unsurpassed speed of movement. The state beyond the body <term>vikaraṇa-bhāvaḥ</term> is the functioning of the senses in relation to desired places, times, and objects, even for those who are disembodied <note>the state where the senses act independently of the physical body</note>. Mastery over the Primary Cause <term>pradhāna-jayaḥ</term> is control over all natural manifestations and their transformations. These three perfections are called the "Honey-Like" <term>madhu-pratīkā</term> perfections. These are attained from the mastery of the five forms of the sense organs. 48

## For one who has only the discernment of the distinction between the intellect and the Spirit, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience. 49

When the stains of passion <term>rajas</term> and darkness <term>tamas</term> are washed away from the intellectual essence <term>buddhi-sattva</term>, the yogi reaches supreme lucidity <term>vaishāradya</term>. In this highest state of self-mastery, established only in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Spirit <term>purusha</term>, comes supremacy over all states of existence. The qualities of nature <term>guṇas</term>, which constitute the essence of all things, appearing as...

---

He speaks of the perfections resulting from the mastery of the five forms of the senses: **From that, there is speed of mind, the state beyond the body, and mastery over the Primary Cause.** The state beyond the body is the functioning of the instruments <note>the senses</note> for those without a physical body. Place refers to regions such as Kashmir and others. Time refers to the past and other times. Object refers to subtle things and others. From the mastery of the senses in their relationship to the body comes mastery over the Primary Cause, which is control over all natural manifestations and their transformations. These perfections are called the "Honey-Like" <term>madhu-pratīkā</term> perfections by those skilled in the science of Yoga. One might ask: if the senses and their objects are mastered through the mastery of the senses, how does mastery over the Primary Cause, which is their cause, follow? He says: **And these.** This refers to the five forms of the instruments, such as perception. The meaning is this: these perfections do not come simply from mastery of the senses, but from mastery of the five forms, which include the Primary Cause and other elements within them. 48

These meditations <term>saṃyama</term> are the causes of powers in the form of knowledge and action. Through the faith generated by the realization of these powers, either directly or indirectly, he shows the intermediate glories of that discernment of the distinction between the intellect and the Spirit: **For one who has only the discernment of the distinction between the intellect and the Spirit, there is supremacy over all states of existence and omniscience.** Lucidity <term>vaishāradya</term> comes from the removal of the stains of passion and darkness. Then comes the highest state of self-mastery. Indeed, the mind-intellect was overwhelmed by passion and darkness and was not under its own control. When those are subsided, it comes under the control of the yogi. When that intellect is controlled, the yogi who is established only in the discernment of the difference between the intellect and the Spirit gains supremacy over all states of existence. He explains this: **The qualities, which constitute the essence of all things...**

<margin>Commentary of Su <note>referring to Su Shi, 1037 to 1101</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but strive for learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Yet, without a way to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "To hear much, select what is good and follow it; to see much and remember it—this is the second level of knowledge." <note>A reference to the Analects 7.28, suggesting that empirical accumulation is inferior to intuitive realization.</note> If one day you know the Way, you will look back on the false and the artificial; nothing there is not delusional. To remove delusion and return to your true nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to <term>Zigong</term> <gloss>a prominent disciple</gloss>: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with one principle." <note>Analects 15.3</note> Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is called "decreasing." Once delusion no longer exists, and one reaches the point of forgetting even this mind to purely return to nature with nothing remaining, then one can depart from "acting" without losing the state of <term>wu-wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have desires to "take" the world through logic and affairs. Thus, they create tasks and seek outcomes, but this is visible to others, and the world dislikes it; therefore, it is difficult and cannot be achieved. The Sage practices non-action and thus his mind is free of affairs. This is visible to others, and the world is at peace with it. Although he does not "take" the world or its affairs, the world and its affairs follow and find peace through him.

<margin>Commentary of Lü <note>likely Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111</note></margin>One who pursues learning is one who has not yet heard the Way. To seek it without hearing it, one must be broad, thus it is said "one increases daily." One who pursues the Way is one who has already heard the Way. Having heard it and practicing it, one must simply practice non-action, thus it is said "one decreases daily." "Decreasing and further decreasing" means one has not yet escaped the state of having action. One must decrease even that which does the decreasing. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action means a state of being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one responds and thus penetrates all the causes of the world. Moving from non-action to reaching the ultimate non-action is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who but the most divine can participate in this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-action. As for those who use "action," it is clear they are not sufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary of Huang Maocai <note>a Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only when there is nothing one does not know can one speak of "learning," therefore learning desires daily increase. Only when there is nothing one does not "do" can one speak of the Way, therefore the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop all attachments to reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their application is inexhaustible; they move through the world with ample room and ease.

<margin>Commentary of Xizhai <note>the pen name of Li Kan, 1245 to 1320</note></margin>Pursuing learning is the means to seek knowledge, hence it increases daily. Pursuing the Way is the means to remove delusion, hence it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, "daily increase" serves as the foundation for "daily decrease." If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is complete, then there is non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never not been "non-action." This is no longer easily discussed in terms of "increase" or "decrease." When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast and manifold, it is unified by one principle. If one tries to manage the world by creating affairs, even a single thing will be entangled and mistaken; how much more so with the many things of the world?

The Sage has no constant <term>xin</term> <gloss>heart-mind</gloss>; he takes the heart-mind of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good. In ancient times, the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> had a thousand officials, and the feudal lords <note>regional rulers</note> had one hundred officials. When a ruler uses these thousand officials to ensure his commands are carried out across all the Chinese states, he is called a King <term>Wang</term> <gloss>a true sovereign who rules by moral authority</gloss>. When a ruler uses these hundred officials to ensure commands are followed within his own borders, then even if the state is not completely secure, it will not reach the point of collapse or ruin <margin>The character for "succeed" <note>遂</note> should be read as "fall" <note>墜</note>, meaning to let one's legacy or state business fall into ruin.</margin>. Such a person is called a Ruler <term>Jun</term> <gloss>a legitimate lord</gloss>.

Consider the descendant of a Sage King. He has inherited the world; he holds the official registers and is the head of the Great House of the realm. However, if he lacks talent and is not upright <margin>Not upright <note>不中</note> means he lacks moral correctness or central balance.</margin>, then internally the common people will resent him, and externally the feudal lords will rebel against him. Those nearby within his borders will not be unified, and those far away will not obey his commands. His orders will not be carried out within his own realm. In extreme cases, the feudal lords will seize his territory and attack him. In such a situation, even if he has not yet perished, I say he "does not possess the world."

When a Sage King has passed away and his successor is weak and incapable of managing affairs <margin>The character for "quit" <note>罷</note> is used here for its sound to mean weak or infirm. "Bind" <note>縣</note> refers to the ability to hold the world together under one's authority.</margin>, the world is effectively without a ruler. If there is a feudal lord who can demonstrate bright virtue and accumulate prestige, the people within the four seas will all desire him as their ruler and teacher. If a cruel state acts with unrestrained indulgence <margin>Cruel states refers to the domains of tyrants like Jie and Zhou. "Unrestrained" refers to their wild and indulgent behavior.</margin>, he will surely punish them. He must not harm the innocent people; he punishes the ruler of the cruel state as if he were punishing a "lone man" <margin>A "lone man" <note>獨夫</note> is a ruler whom the world has abandoned, leaving him with no more support than a single common person.</margin>. If he acts in this way, he can be said to be able to employ the world. One who can employ the world is called a King.

Tang and Wu <note>Kings Tang of Shang and Wu of Zhou, traditional examples of virtuous founders</note> did not "seize" the world. They cultivated the Way and practiced righteousness. They shared the same interests as the world and removed what the world found harmful; thus, the world turned to them. Jie and Zhou <note>The final, tyrannical rulers of the Xia and Shang dynasties</note> did not "lose" the world by choice. Rather, they turned against the virtue of Yu and Tang, disrupted the distinctions of ritual and righteousness, and acted like beasts. Their wickedness accumulated, and their subjects abandoned them <margin>This implies the world left them of its own accord.</margin>.

<summary>Xunzi defines true kingship not by title or inheritance, but by the ability to maintain order through virtue and the support of the people. ### Commentary on the Brahma Sutras | Chapter 3, Part 3, Adhikarana 7, Sutra 14

For it is established that the Supreme is taught as being superior to all of these together; it is not the case that the superiority of each of these individual stages is being taught. Why is that? Because there is a lack of purpose. No purpose is seen or heard in scripture regarding the knowledge of the senses and the rest as being superior in themselves. However, a purpose is seen—namely, the attainment of <term>Moksha</term> <gloss>Liberation</gloss>—when the <term>Purusha</term> <gloss>Pure Consciousness/Supreme Person</gloss>, who is superior to the senses and beyond the entire path of worldly objects, is realized. Thus, the <term>Shruti</term> <gloss>Revealed Scripture</gloss> says: "By perceiving That, one is released from the jaws of death" <note>Katha Upanishad 3.15</note>. Furthermore, by using the word <term>kastha</term> <gloss>the goal or limit</gloss> and by negating anything beyond it, the scripture shows its primary regard for the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the entire sequence of prior and subsequent stages is for the sake of realizing the <term>Purusha</term>. Regarding the word "for the sake of the narrative" <note>Sanskrit: akhyanaya</note> in the sutra: it means for the sake of right vision, which is preceded by the narrative. This narrative is taught only for the sake of right vision, and the narrative itself is not the primary subject. ॥ 14 ॥

**And because of the word Atman <gloss>the Self</gloss>. ॥ 15 ॥**

For this reason also, the mention of the sequence of the senses and the rest is only for the realization of the <term>Purusha</term>. The reason is that the scripture refers to the <term>Purusha</term> under discussion as the <term>Atman</term> <gloss>Self</gloss>, saying: "This <term>Atman</term> is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth; but it is seen by those of subtle vision through their sharp and subtle intellect" <note>Katha Upanishad 3.12</note>. From this, it is understood that the intention is to describe the non-selfhood of the others. The text also shows the difficulty of knowing it and that it is attainable by a refined intellect. For the sake of knowing that <term>Atman</term>, the scripture provides the instruction: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind" <note>Katha Upanishad 3.13</note>. This was already explained in the section "Even if it is based on inference for some" <note>Brahma Sutra 1.4.1</note>. In this way, through various methods, there is a great significance in the beginning and the underlying intention.

**Bhamati** <note>Sub-commentary by Vacaspati Mishra</note>

Moreover, the Veda, by using the sign of negating anything higher in the phrase "That is the goal," and by the sign of the <term>Purusha</term> being superior to all states of being, shows that the focus is on the <term>Purusha</term>. It shows that the statement of one thing being superior to the previous one is for that purpose. This is the meaning of the phrase "Moreover..." The author of the Sutras connects this by saying "for the sake of the narrative," meaning that since the objects and so on have no purpose in themselves, their superiority is stated only to facilitate the vision of the <term>Purusha</term> through that narrative ॥ 14 ॥ Regarding "And because of the word Atman": Furthermore, because there is a uniformity between the beginning "That is the highest step of Vishnu" and the conclusion "There is nothing higher than the <term>Purusha</term>," and because it is determined to be a single unified teaching focused on the one <term>Purusha</term> which yields the fruit of liberation, it is not proper to imagine separate sentences or separate fruits, as that would be unnecessarily complex ॥ 15 ॥

**Nyaya Nirnaya** <note>Sub-commentary by Anandagiri</note>

To the question "Why?", the author explains that because there is no fruit or purpose in knowing the superiority of the senses and the rest, they are not intended to be the objects of knowledge. He says "No purpose..." To the doubt that a purpose might be established through logic or scripture, he denies the first by saying "No," and the second by saying "nor is it heard." Since this context is seen to be about the Ultimate Reality, it is not proper to treat it as a command for meditation. When it is possible to treat it as being about the knowledge of the Supreme Goal, it is not proper to assume it is about the senses or other goals established by memory or other systems. Even if the knowledge of the <term>Purusha</term>'s superiority is not the fruit itself, the author explains that because it is an infinite object characterized by the absence of worldly objects, the indestructibility of the desire for the <term>Purusha</term> is established by experience. He says "In the <term>Purusha</term>, however..." Since the destruction of ignorance and delusion is a seen result, it is not proper to imagine an unseen result. He cites scripture for those who disagree. Furthermore, he explains why this entire context is focused on the knowledge of the <term>Purusha</term>. The Veda shows regard for the <term>Purusha</term> by the sign of negating anything higher and the word "limit." The mention of the prior and subsequent flow refers to the superiority of each subsequent thing over the previous one. Since there is no command for meditation here, how can the knowledge of the Supreme <term>Purusha</term> be for meditation? Explaining the part of the sutra, he says "narrative." Even the knowledge of the <term>Brahman</term> without qualities is for the sake of meditation because it resides in <term>Brahman</term>. He denies this, saying "right vision," as it would contradict scriptures that say "then one sees Him." ॥ 14 ॥ He gives another reason why only the <term>Purusha</term> is taught as being superior to all in the sutra "And because of the word Atman." He explains the word "and" in the sutra. Clarifying this, he breaks down the word <term>Atman</term>. He removes the doubt that the <term>Atman</term> is naturally non-luminous by citing "it is seen." He says that in that very scripture, it is called <term>Atman</term>. He explains the intended meaning of the words in the sutra. He explains that it is attainable by a refined intellect. He gives the reason implied by the word "and." Simply restraining speech is heard in the verse, not a command for meditation. He says "that was explained." Because the <term>Atman</term> is difficult to know through scripture and is unknown, and because the senses and the rest are easy to understand, the statement of their superiority is also intended for the knowledge of the <term>Atman</term>. There is a great significance in the beginning and the underlying intention.

<summary>This page argues that the hierarchy of the senses and mind in the Katha Upanishad is intended solely to lead to the knowledge of the Supreme Purusha or Atman, rather than being an end in itself. Shankara and his commentators emphasize that only the realization of the Self leads to the fruit of liberation.</summary>

# Section 44: The Superintendent of Courtesans

A courtesan who refuses to visit a man when commanded by the king shall receive one thousand lashes with a whip, or she shall pay a fine of five thousand <term>panas</term> <gloss>standard copper coins</gloss>.

If a courtesan shows dislike toward a client after having accepted her fee, she shall be fined double the amount of that fee.

If a man takes away the residence of a courtesan or withholds her fee, he shall pay a fine eight times the amount of the fee, except in cases involving the man's own physical defects or if the courtesan is suffering from a disease.

For a courtesan who causes the death of a man by over-confinement or by drowning him in water, the punishment shall be death by drowning.

Anyone who steals the jewelry or the fee of a courtesan shall be fined eight times the value of the stolen items.

A courtesan shall report to the authorities her fee, her projected income, and the identity of the man she is with.

By these regulations, the rules governing the wives of actors, dancers, singers, musicians, professional storytellers, bards, rope-dancers, magicians, and wandering minstrels, as well as women who trade in their own beauty and those who live as clandestine prostitutes, are explained.

Visiting musical troupes among these performers shall pay a fee of five <term>panas</term> for each public performance.

Common prostitutes <note>original: <term>rūpājīvā</term></note> shall pay a tax to the state equal to two days' earnings every month.

The state shall ensure that courtesans, female slaves, and actresses are trained in the arts of singing, instrumental music, recitation, dancing, acting, writing, painting, playing the lute, flute, and drum, reading the thoughts of others, preparing perfumes and garlands, the art of charming, grooming, and the various skills of the bedroom <note>original: <term>vaiśika-kalā</term></note>. Their livelihood shall be provided by the royal court. The sons of courtesans and theater performers shall be trained as the primary teachers of the arts for other performers and for those who manage musical timing <note>original: <term>tāla</term></note>.

Women who are skilled in secret signals and foreign languages shall be employed to spy upon, assassinate, or cause the downfall of foreign enemies, using their relatives and transport as cover.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Superintendent of Courtesans," in the section on the Activities of Superintendents.

This is the forty-eighth chapter from the beginning of the work.

# Srimad Bhagavad Gita

[Chapter 9, Verses 30-31]

### Shreedhara’s Commentary
If you give liberation only to your devotees and not to those who are not devotees, then is there a partiality in you caused by attachment and aversion? To this the Lord says "I am equal" <note>This refers to the preceding Verse 29: "I am equal in all beings..."</note>. I am equal in all beings. Therefore, there is no one who is particularly hateful or dear to me. Even though this is true, those who worship me with devotion abide in me, and I also abide in them as their benefactor. The meaning is this: Fire removes the distress of darkness and cold only for those who stay near it, yet the fire itself has no partiality. Similarly, the wish-fulfilling tree <term>kalpavriksha</term> <gloss>a divine tree that grants all desires</gloss> acts without bias. In the same way, even though I favor my devotees, I have no partiality. This is simply the supreme greatness of devotion to me. || 29 ||

### Madhusudana’s Commentary
Furthermore, the greatness of devotion to me is such that it brings about a distinction even in one who is equal to all. Hear its greatness—

> Even if a person of extremely evil conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he must be considered a righteous person, for he has made a right resolution. || 30 ||

If anyone, even one of very evil conduct like Ajamila <note>A famous figure in the Puranas who was a great sinner but was saved by calling upon the name of God</note> and others, worships me with undivided devotion due to some dawn of good fortune, he must be considered righteous, even if he was unrighteous before. This is because he has made a right resolution <note>original: "samya-vyavasitah"</note>; he possesses the firm conviction of a saintly person. || 30 ||

### Shreedhara’s Commentary
Furthermore, showing the inconceivable influence of devotion to me, the Lord says: "Even if." Even a man of extremely evil conduct, if he worships me—the Lord Narayana—alone, without practicing devotion to other deities separately, then he must be considered excellent and righteous. This is because he has made a right resolution. He has made a beautiful determination, thinking, "I shall become successful and fulfilled only by the worship of the Supreme Lord." || 30 ||

### Madhusudana’s Commentary
Because of this very right resolution, having abandoned his evil conduct—

> Quickly he becomes a righteous soul and attains eternal peace. O son of Kunti <term>Kaunteya</term> <gloss>Arjuna</gloss>, declare it boldly: my devotee never perishes. || 31 ||

Even if one has been an unrighteous soul for a long time, by the greatness of worshiping me, he "quickly"—meaning very soon—becomes a righteous soul <term>dharmatma</term> <gloss>one whose mind follows the path of virtue</gloss>. The meaning is that after immediately abandoning evil conduct, he becomes a person of good conduct. Furthermore, he "attains eternal peace," which is the complete cessation of the desire for sensual enjoyments due to intense detachment. If someone suggests that my devotee might not become a righteous soul, might not give up his previous evil conduct, and thus would surely perish, the Lord says "no." Being overcome by compassion for his devotees, the Lord speaks as if he were angry: "O son of Kunti <term>Kaunteya</term>, do not think this is a miracle. Such is the established greatness of my devotion. Therefore, even in front of those who disagree, you should declare it. Make a promise with disregard for the doubters and with pride: 'The devotee of me, Vasudeva <note>Krishna</note>, even if he was of very evil conduct, even if he has fallen into a life-threatening crisis, even if he is sought after for a high position, even if he is very foolish or without refuge—he does not perish. Instead, he becomes one who has achieved the goal of his life.'"

<note>Footnote 1: Manuscripts labeled Ka, Ga, Gha, Nga, Cha, Chha, Ja, and Jha read "beautifully resolved" </note><note>original: "shobhanam"</note> as a variant for "rightly resolved."

In this context, this refers to hunters and others who kill for worldly purposes. The word <term>paśughna</term> <gloss>animal-killer</gloss> is a Vedic grammatical form.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa:** "So many times" means that specific number of occurrences. A "vain killer" is one not authorized by the Vedas or traditional law.

( 3 ) **Kullūka:** He who kills animals for his own sake without intending them for a deity is called a "vain killer." ( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda:** He describes the punishment for the opposing view. Here, the word <term>ha</term> highlights a well-known fact.

( 5 ) **Nandana:** "So many times" means that many instances. The word <term>ha</term> is used here to express compassion.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra:** A man who kills an animal in vain performs an unrighteous act of killing in this world. For as many hairs as there are—estimated at eighty million hairs—he will attain the state of an animal and experience death for that many times in birth after birth in the afterlife.

By this, it is said that there is no fault because by the sacrifice of one animal, many living beings are sustained.

He shall be made to return that <term>upanidhi</term> <gloss>open deposit</gloss> with its increase <note>interest</note> to the owner—with interest in the case of personal use, or with the profit in the case of trading. The standard for interest was stated by <term>Katyayana</term> <gloss>a legal commentator</gloss>: "If a deposit, a balance of interest, a purchase, or a sale is not returned when demanded, it shall increase at five percent <note>per month</note>." # Samkhya-tattva-vritti

The Higher <note>the supreme or transcendental aspect</note> is the Great Lord, the omniscient creator and mother of the entire universe. How is he to be known? Either through inference or through effort. For instance: the perceived world, which is the subject of dispute, has a cause, because it has come into being and continues to exist, like a painting; this is the inference. From this general understanding, specific knowledge arises through <term>yoga</term> <gloss>disciplined practice</gloss>. The existence of the other, the <term>jīva</term> <gloss>individual soul</gloss>, is established through one's own experience alone. The activity of <term>prakṛti</term> <gloss>primal nature</gloss> is for the purpose of the discriminative knowledge of these two, the higher and the lower. In this context, its "purpose for another" <note>the soul</note> will be explained. As for its "own purpose," once it has shown itself to a <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>spirit/consciousness</gloss> through discrimination, it becomes indifferent toward that spirit. How can unconscious nature act? It is observed that even unconscious things, like milk and the like, act for the sake of a result <note>such as the nourishment of a calf</note>. || 1 ||

Now, as to who is eligible for <term>mokṣa</term> <gloss>liberation</gloss>, it is said:

**It is accomplished for one who is dispassionate.** || 2 ||

And thus the <term>śruti</term> <gloss>scripture</gloss> says: "Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then lead the life of a mendicant" <note>original: "putraiṣaṇāyāśca vittaiṣaṇāyāśca lokaiṣaṇāyāśca vyutthāya atha bhikṣācaryam caranti"</note>; and "Becoming calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one sees the Self in the Self alone" <note>original: "śānto dānta uparatastitikṣuḥ samāhito bhūtvā ātmani eva ātmānam paśyati"</note>. || 2 ||

If liberation occurs because of <term>vairāgya</term> <gloss>dispassion</gloss> immediately after hearing the teachings, then liberation should occur for everyone after the Guru’s instruction. However, this is not seen to be the case. To this he says:

**Its accomplishment does not come from hearing alone, because beginningless latent impressions are powerful.** || 3 ||

Liberation does not follow immediately after hearing; rather, because of the strength of beginningless <term>vāsanā</term> <gloss>latent impressions</gloss>, liberation is swift for some and takes a long time for others. || 3 ||

He states another reason:

**Because of multiplicity, [the effect is] individual to each.** || 4 ||

### 3. Revealing the Characteristics of Conditioned Arising
This refers to the phrase concerning the polluted minds.

#### The Heading
There are six kinds of polluted mind.

#### The Inquiry
What are the six?

Within each of the six, there are two aspects: first, the obstacle, and second, the remedy.

#### The Explanation
However, these six pollutions are correlated in reverse order with the six coarse aspects <note>from the Awakening of Faith</note>: the first four of the six pollutions match the first four coarse aspects, while the last three subtle aspects... Since this volume follows the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, where the coarse aspects consist of sections three and four, there are only six here. These names are borrowed to categorize these six.

#### 1. The Aspect of Attachment-Apprehension and the Reckoning of Names
First is the **pollution associated with attachment**. It is distanced <note>eliminated</note> through the liberation of the two vehicles <note>Sravakas and Pratyekabuddhas</note> and the Stage of Correspondence with Faith.

This corresponds to the third and fourth aspects among the six coarse ones. It also refers to the growth of the afflictions of "views" <note>intellectual errors</note> and "craving" <note>emotional attachments</note> in the conscious mind. It is also the "aspect of the attachment of discrimination" among the four aspects mentioned above. Since the coarse mind externally attaches to and corresponds with objects, polluting pure conduct, it is called pollution. Regarding the "liberation of the two vehicles," this reaches the <term>Asaiksha</term> <gloss>the stage of no-more-learning, or Arhatship</gloss>, where the afflictions of views and cultivation are completely abandoned. "Correspondence with Faith" refers to the stages from the Ten Dwellings onward, where the root of faith is perfected and there is no falling back. Thus, it is called Correspondence with Faith. As the *Treatise on the Ten Stages* says: The stages before the <term>Bhumis</term> <gloss>the ten grounds of a Bodhisattva</gloss> are collectively called the Stage of Practicing Faith. Asanga's *Treatise on Non-attachment* <note>the Mahayanasamgraha</note> also contains this same explanation. This Bodhisattva

attains the realization of the emptiness of the person <term>pudgala-sunyata</term>, so that the afflictions of views and cultivation no longer manifest; therefore, it is called "distanced." This does not refer to the removal of latent tendencies <term>anusaya</term> <gloss>underlying seeds of affliction</gloss>, as Bodhisattvas "retain the seeds of affliction" <note>to remain in the cycle of birth and death to help others</note>. The *Compendium of the Great Vehicle* <note>Mahayanasamgraha</note> says: If one does not cut off the manifest mind, one is no different from an ordinary person; if one does not retain the seeds of affliction, one is no different from the two vehicles. Furthermore, the two intentions for retaining affliction are for the benefit of oneself and others. This is the explanation according to the Final Teaching <note>the Huayan classification of the highest Mahayana</note>. If according to the Initial Teaching, it is only from the First Stage <note>the First Bhumi</note> upward that the "retention of affliction" is discussed, as mentioned in other treatises. Here, this Bodhisattva does not simply cut off the four dwellings of attachment to a self, but also partially cuts off the "ground of the dwelling of ignorance." Therefore, this treatise says below: "Those who do not understand the meaning of the single Dharma-realm" are those who contemplate and learn to cut it off from the Stage of Correspondence with Faith. Here, the text only intends to reveal the coarseness of the "ego-self" <note>attachment to a personal soul</note>, so the other aspects are not discussed.

#### 2. The Aspect of Continuity
Second is the **pollution associated with non-interruption**. It is gradually abandoned through the skillful means of study and practice in the Stage of Correspondence with Faith, and completely abandoned upon attaining the Stage of the Pure Heart <note>the first Bhumi, or Stage of Joy</note>.

This is the second of the six coarse aspects. From this point to the sixth, they are again correlated in reverse order with the five aspects of mind; this position corresponds to the fifth mind aspect. It simply refers to the attachment to phenomena <term>dharma</term> continuing to arise without interruption; this is the meaning of "continuity." From the Ten Dwellings onward, using the "consciousness-only" contemplation of investigation and analysis as a skillful means, up until the first stage where one realizes the three-fold non-nature <note>the lack of inherent existence in three aspects</note> and the pervasive True Suchness, the "discrimination of attachment to phenomena" no longer manifests.

#### 3. The Aspect of Intelligence
Third is the **pollution associated with discriminating intelligence**. It is gradually distanced from the Stage of Perfect Precepts <note>the second Bhumi</note> and completely distanced at the Stage of Skillful Means of Signlessness <note>the seventh Bhumi</note>.

This is the first of the six coarse aspects and the fourth of the five mind aspects. Because it can discriminate between the mundane and the supramundane, and between the polluted and the pure, it is called "intelligence." This is the "affliction of cultivation" <note>the deeper, habitual delusions</note> regarding attachment to phenomena. Because there is still a difference between entering and exiting meditative contemplation before the seventh stage, there is subtle discrimination regarding objects. ### Section Seven: Nothing Obtained, Nothing Spoken

Subhuti! What do you think? Has the Tathagata attained <term>Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi</term> <gloss>Supreme, Perfect Enlightenment</gloss>? Has the Tathagata spoken any Law?

Subhuti replied: As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed Law called <term>Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi</term>, nor is there any fixed Law that the Tathagata can speak. Why is this? The Law spoken by the Tathagata cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken. It is not the Law, yet it is not not the Law. Why is this so? All worthy and holy beings are distinguished by the <term>unconditioned Law</term> <gloss>asamskrta; reality that is eternal and not produced by causes</gloss>.

### Section Eight: Born from the Law

Subhuti! What do you think? If a person filled <term>three thousand great thousand worlds</term> <gloss>a vast Buddhist cosmological system representing a universe</gloss> with the <term>seven treasures</term> <gloss>precious materials including gold, silver, and lapis lazuli</gloss> to give as <term>charity</term> <gloss>dana</gloss>, would the <term>merit</term> <gloss>punya; spiritual credit</gloss> gained by this person be great?

Subhuti said: Very great, <term>World-Honored One</term> <gloss>Bhagavan</gloss>! Why? This merit does not have the nature of merit. Therefore, the Tathagata says that the merit is great.

If, however, there is someone who receives and maintains even a <term>four-line verse</term> <gloss>gatha</gloss> from this sutra and explains it to others, their merit would surpass the former. Why? Subhuti! All Buddhas and the Law of Supreme, Perfect Enlightenment of all Buddhas emerge from this sutra. Subhuti! That which is called the Buddha's Law is not, in fact, the Buddha's Law.

○ <term>Zi Xia</term> <gloss>a prominent disciple of Confucius known for his scholarship</gloss> said: "If a person honors the worthy as worthy <note>original: 賢賢, xian xian</note> and changes his regard for physical beauty <note>original: 易色, yi se</note>; if in serving his parents he can exhaust his strength; if in serving his lord he can devote his life; and if in interacting with friends his words are trustworthy—even if it is said that such a person has not yet studied, I will certainly say that he has."

<term>Zi Xia</term> was a disciple of Confucius. His surname was Bu and his name was Shang; he was a man from the state of Wei. To "honor the worthy as worthy and change his regard for physical beauty" means to appreciate the virtue of the worthy and thereby transform the heart that loves physical beauty. It refers to the beauty of loving goodness. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi, the primary commentator</note> said that the Master twice remarked on never having seen anyone love virtue as much as they love physical beauty. The <term>Zhongyong</term> <gloss>Doctrine of the Mean</gloss> also treats distancing oneself as a method for dealing with physical beauty. "Devote" <note>original: 致, zhi</note> is similar to "entrust" <note>original: 委, wei</note>. To entrust and devote one's life means to no longer treat the body as one's private possession. Sincerity lies in changing the love of beauty. Therefore, the explanation by Fan <note>Fan Zuyu, a Song dynasty historian and scholar</note> is the most accurate.
